title: SQL Day 11 — Multi-Step CTE Analysis & Reusable Business Logic
description: Turn complex business requests into readable SQL pipelines by chaining CTEs, separating calculation layers, and combining multiple intermediate datasets into one decision-ready result.

topics.title: Chained CTEs — Build an Analysis Pipeline
topics.business_skill: Break a business request into sequential named transformations that can be tested and reused.

teaching.teacher:
## Chained CTEs
A query can define multiple CTEs separated by commas. Each CTE can reference earlier CTEs, creating a readable analysis pipeline.
teaching.explain: Use one CTE for each meaningful business transformation: for example, calculate customer sales first, then classify those customers, then summarize the classifications.
teaching.detailedlearning: Design the grain of every CTE before writing SQL. Give each layer one responsibility and reference earlier layers by name instead of repeating the same calculation.
teaching.expose: A long query becomes easier to validate when intermediate business logic has explicit names such as customer_sales, customer_segment, or regional_summary.
teaching.example: WITH customer_sales AS (SELECT customer_name,SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY customer_name), customer_class AS (SELECT customer_name,total_sales,CASE WHEN total_sales>=5000 THEN 'High Value' ELSE 'Standard' END AS value_class FROM customer_sales) SELECT value_class,COUNT(*) AS customers,SUM(total_sales) AS sales FROM customer_class GROUP BY value_class;
teaching.business_question: The customer director wants customers classified by total sales and then summarized by value class.
teaching.expected_sql: WITH customer_sales AS (SELECT customer_name,SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY customer_name), customer_class AS (SELECT customer_name,total_sales,CASE WHEN total_sales>=5000 THEN 'High Value' ELSE 'Standard' END AS value_class FROM customer_sales) SELECT value_class,COUNT(*) AS customers,SUM(total_sales) AS sales FROM customer_class GROUP BY value_class;

topics.title: CTE + JOIN — Combine Prepared Business Layers
topics.business_skill: Prepare an aggregated dataset in a CTE and join it to master data for business context.

teaching.teacher:
## CTE plus JOIN
A CTE can create a clean analytical layer before it is joined to another table. This separates metric calculation from descriptive attributes.
teaching.explain: For example, calculate customer sales from orders in one CTE and then join that result to the customer master to add segment or region.
teaching.detailedlearning: Aggregate the transactional table at the required grain before joining when the business question asks for one row per customer. This prevents accidental duplication.
teaching.expose: The join should enrich a prepared metric, not silently change its grain. Validate row counts and keys after the join.
teaching.example: WITH customer_sales AS (SELECT customer_name,SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY customer_name) SELECT c.customer_name,c.segment,cs.total_sales FROM customers c JOIN customer_sales cs ON c.customer_name=cs.customer_name;
teaching.business_question: Customer leadership wants sales totals enriched with customer segment.
teaching.expected_sql: WITH customer_sales AS (SELECT customer_name,SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY customer_name) SELECT c.customer_name,c.segment,cs.total_sales FROM customers c JOIN customer_sales cs ON c.customer_name=cs.customer_name;

topics.title: CTE Benchmarks — Compare Business Groups to an Overall Benchmark
topics.business_skill: Create a grouped KPI layer and compare each group against a benchmark calculated from that layer.

teaching.teacher:
## CTE benchmark pattern
First calculate the business metric at the required grain. Then calculate a benchmark from that prepared result and compare each group against it.
teaching.explain: This avoids averaging raw transactions when the business actually wants an average of group totals.
teaching.detailedlearning: Keep the metric grain explicit: region-level, category-level, or customer-level. Use a second CTE for the benchmark so the final comparison is readable.
teaching.expose: The benchmark must be calculated from the same grain as the values being compared.
teaching.example: WITH regional_sales AS (SELECT region,SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region), benchmark AS (SELECT AVG(total_sales) AS avg_region_sales FROM regional_sales) SELECT r.region,r.total_sales,b.avg_region_sales FROM regional_sales r CROSS JOIN benchmark b WHERE r.total_sales>b.avg_region_sales;
teaching.business_question: The director wants regions whose sales exceed the average regional sales total.
teaching.expected_sql: WITH regional_sales AS (SELECT region,SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region), benchmark AS (SELECT AVG(total_sales) AS avg_region_sales FROM regional_sales) SELECT r.region,r.total_sales,b.avg_region_sales FROM regional_sales r CROSS JOIN benchmark b WHERE r.total_sales>b.avg_region_sales;

questions.validation: Regional aggregation CTE + benchmark CTE + comparison

topics.title: Multiple Analytical Layers — From Transaction Data to Decision KPI
topics.business_skill: Translate a multi-step stakeholder request into separate data-preparation, classification, and KPI layers.

teaching.teacher:
## Multi-layer SQL
A production analytical query often has several logical stages: clean or aggregate the base data, add business classifications, then summarize the resulting population.
teaching.explain: The goal is not to make SQL longer. The goal is to make each business transformation independently understandable and testable.
teaching.detailedlearning: Write the business steps in plain language first, then map each step to a CTE. Avoid mixing transaction-level and summary-level logic unless the grain is intentional.
teaching.expose: This pattern is the bridge from ad-hoc SQL to maintainable analytical SQL used in reporting and BI pipelines.
teaching.example: WITH product_sales AS (SELECT product_name,category,SUM(sales) AS total_sales,SUM(profit) AS total_profit FROM orders GROUP BY product_name,category), product_status AS (SELECT product_name,category,total_sales,total_profit,CASE WHEN total_profit<0 THEN 'Loss' WHEN total_profit/NULLIF(total_sales,0)<0.10 THEN 'Low Margin' ELSE 'Healthy' END AS status FROM product_sales) SELECT category,status,COUNT(*) AS products,SUM(total_sales) AS sales FROM product_status GROUP BY category,status;
teaching.business_question: Product leadership wants products classified by profitability and summarized by category.
teaching.expected_sql: Build a product-level CTE, classify each product by profit/margin, then summarize products and sales by category and status.

topics.title: Refactoring Complex SQL — Replace Repeated Logic with CTEs
topics.business_skill: Improve analytical SQL maintainability by eliminating duplicated subqueries and giving repeated business calculations one definition.

teaching.teacher:
## SQL refactoring with CTEs
When the same calculation appears multiple times, a CTE can define it once and let several later steps reference it.
teaching.explain: Refactoring is an analytical engineering skill: the result should remain correct while the query becomes easier to read, test, and modify.
teaching.detailedlearning: Identify repeated logic, extract it into a named CTE, then build the final query from that shared layer. Preserve the original business grain.
teaching.expose: Readable SQL reduces maintenance risk when a KPI definition changes. One named metric layer is easier to update than several copied expressions.
teaching.example: WITH category_kpi AS (SELECT category,SUM(sales) AS total_sales,SUM(profit) AS total_profit FROM orders GROUP BY category) SELECT category,total_sales,total_profit,total_profit/NULLIF(total_sales,0) AS profit_margin FROM category_kpi ORDER BY profit_margin DESC;
teaching.business_question: Finance wants one reusable category KPI layer containing sales, profit, and margin.
teaching.expected_sql: WITH category_kpi AS (SELECT category,SUM(sales) AS total_sales,SUM(profit) AS total_profit FROM orders GROUP BY category) SELECT category,total_sales,total_profit,total_profit/NULLIF(total_sales,0) AS profit_margin FROM category_kpi ORDER BY profit_margin DESC;
